newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Angolan government rejects UNITA Italy talks offer.
newsitem.headline: Angolan government rejects UNITA Italy talks offer.

text.p: The Angolan government has rejected a UNITA offer to hold talks in Italy on renewed fighting in the northeast of the country, a spokesman for the Angolan embassy in Lisbon said on Saturday.

Spokesman Jose Ribeiro told Reuters that President Jose Eduardo dos Santos had sent a letter to UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan saying that any meeting between himself and UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi outside Angola would be "inopportune".
Ribeiro said the UN Security Council had recommended that any talks between the two leaders should take place in Luanda.

Diplomatic sources in Lisbon said Luanda had also sent a letter to the UN's Special Representative for Angola, Alioune Blondin Beye, asking the UN to issue an immediate declaration calling on the rebel movement not to commit acts that could delay the fragile peace process.

The fighting, which has flared up in the diamond-rich northeast of the country, is threatening to restart a civil war that went on for 20 years until the 1994 Lusaka accords brought about a shaky peace.

Military sources say the government and UNITA have thrown many troops into recent battles. The army was using tanks and artillery and the ex-rebels were firing mortar barrages in what was described as the worst fighting since the peace pact was signed.

The outbreak is directly linked to last month's defeat of Mobutu Sese Seko in neighbouring Zaire, a longtime ally of UNITA. Mobutu was toppled by Laurent Kabila, who has the staunch support of the Angolan government.

On Friday UNITA said Savimbi was prepared to meet Dos Santos in Italy where the Angolan president is on holiday. The offer was in response to an appeal from Kofi Annan for talks "with the precise aim of overcoming the current deep crisis".
In its first official statement since the fighting began three weeks ago, the Angolan government said on Friday that UNITA was gathering soldiers and war material, threatening the peace accord.

"The United Nations must adopt measures to stop these belligerent intentions...the government has no intention of returning to war...the government cannot ignore its own responsibilities to secure the frontier," it said.

The government denies it is taking advantage of UNITA's loss of a major ally who guarded the rebel movement's back door beyond the northern Angolan border with Zaire, and gave it logistics routes and a market for diamonds.

But analysts say it has seized the opportunity to roll back UNITA's grip on the northern diamond areas which yield hundreds of millions of dollars annually, if not to deliver a military knockout blow to its old enemy.

Thousands of UNITA troops were reportedly returning to Angola from the former Zaire, where they made a vain bid to prop up the Mobutu regime. Hutu militiamen who fled Rwanda and took refuge in Mobutu's Zaire were said to be among them.
